idiom_name: delegated property (by map / by flag()) and a one-method Toggle interface
implementation_notes: Kotlin keeps the decision at the edge: a delegated property resolves the flag from a configuration map on each read (`val newCheckout: Boolean by values` uses the property name as the key), so the toggle point stays a boolean expression and the router is a ReadOnlyProperty of two lines; a one-method Toggle interface (or a lambda) injected as a constructor parameter is the decision object, keeping services unaware of where the state lives. Configuration comes from wherever the JVM already looks - System.getProperty/getenv, a HOCON or YAML file bound into a data class - and the heavier library form (Togglz, or a vendor SDK) is justified only for targeting, percentage rollout or an admin UI. The classic router is also the right answer when the same flag must be evaluated consistently per request, which a per-read delegate does not guarantee.
pitfalls: Map delegation uses the property name as the key, so renaming a property silently changes the flag key unless the map is built from the same names.
A delegated read with a missing key throws NoSuchElementException: use values.withDefault { false } (or an explicit default) so an absent flag means off rather than a crash.
A val that reads a JVM system property captures the value when the object is constructed; flipping a property later has no effect on that instance.
Because the delegate re-reads on each access, the same request can see two different values if a flip happens mid-request; snapshot the decision where that matters.
